analytic.title: Dynamic Optimal Control for Aperiodic Soft Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper studies the aperiodic soft Real-Time Systems (RTS) with random task arrival and unpredictable task execution time, and proposes a dynamic optimal control model based on the queuing theory. Firstly, we construct a dynamic optimal control model for the FCFS (First Come First Served) scheduling strategy; then, we present a more useful model for DM (Deadline Monotonic) scheduling algorithm. This model can statistically guarantee the schedulability of soft RTS, at the same time it can guarantee the QoS (Quality of Service) of incoming tasks and improve the system throughput. Finally, an example shows that the model is capable of improving the systems performance and it is an efficient workload management method.
I.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the increasingly applications of soft RTS, the aperiodic dynamic task also requires the timeliness guarantee. Examples include video conferencing, on-line trading, C41, and process control, etc.. The main features of such systems are the randomicity of task arrivals and the unpredictability of execution times. Consequently, it's difficult to accurately describe the system behavior and predict the computation result.

It is known that traditional real-time scheduling theory is based on the worst-case analysis, which assumes that the invocations from a task had deterministic periodic, maximum execution times, and minimum deadlines [1]. Based on this assumption, the sufficient condition of scheduling the periodic task set, under a certain algorithm, can be deduced. However, this assumption is not usually reasonable for aperiodic soft RTS. From one aspect, such systems usually run in unpredictable environment [2], [4] and the task execution time may be much greater or less than its mean execution time, which may cause to serious overload or underload [2]. From another aspect, the task arrivals are stochastic, which will lead to the unpredictability of system load. Thus, it is possible that there could be a peak utilization time at which all tasks are simultaneously operating at their peak level, and it also means that some of those tasks would miss their deadlines [3]. Consequently, the worst-case analysis is not suitable for the aperiodic task model, and it is necessary to improve the traditional methods.

This paper, based on the queuing theory, considers the soft RTS in which the task arrival and its execution time are both random, and then proposes a new dynamic control model. We first provide some conclusions upon FCFS scheduling policy, and then construct an optimal control model under DM scheduling policy. Finally, an example, implemented on the CRTOS II, shows that the model can achieve better performance, in comparison with those models not using the optimal control.

For aperiodic tasks, the DM scheduling policy is an important real-time scheduling algorithm [5]. Because of the complexity of aperiodic task scheduling, there is no good method to deal with the aperiodic task scheduling until Tarek F. Adbelzaher proposes the DM algorithm and its necessary condition for schedulability in 2004 [5]. Other scheduling algorithms for aperiodic tasks include: PS (Polling Server), DS (Deferrable Server), SLA (Slack Stealing Algorithms), and LCM (Least Common Multiple), etc.. However, all the above algorithms require the task's accurate execution time a prior.

The Real-Time Queuing Theory (RTQT) is one of the important methods to analyze the RTS. Lehoczky first proposed RTQT in [2]. Doytchinov [6], Kruk [7], and Yeung [8] further improved and enriched the theory and analyzed the mean performance of RTS under heavy load. In addition, T.-S. Tia [9], and A. Atlas [10] did some research on the task queue with variable execution time in order to guarantee the system performance. Kim [11], and J. L. Diaz [12] studied how to statistically ensure the task's deadline on the basis of Markov model.

As far as the random control is concerned, Y. Lu [13], and Henrisksson [14] integrated MIMI1 queuing system with classical control theory to control the task delay of web services, in which the queuing theory is used to predict the task arrival and the control theory is applied to dynamically adjust the task's parameter. This idea works well in the delay and relative delay control. Besides this, L. Sha [15] also used MIMI1 queuing model to predict the task arrival, and then used a PID (Proportional Integral Differential) controller to regulate the system performance.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the task model. Section III introduces the design of the control system, which includes 3 subsections: the optimal control for FCFS, the optimal control for DM and the complexity of the control model. Section IV provides an example to demonstrate the efficiency of the optimal control model, and the last section presents the conclusion of this paper.

div.head: II. TASK MODEL
div.p: In the aperiodic soft RTS, a request is regarded as a task Ti with the arrival time Ai, the execution time Ci, and the relative deadline Di (Fig. 1). The tasks are independent with each other and have no precedence constraints. The task's execution time is variable due to the unpredictable environment. The longer the execution time is, the higher reward the task achieves. The response time is a time interval that a task stays in the system and is described with di. When di < Di, the task timeliness is satisfied, else its deadline is missed. Consequently, a metric, deadline miss ratio m, is used to define the ratio between the tasks that miss their deadlines and the total number oftask.

div.head: III. DESIGN OF THE CONTROL SYSTEM
div.p: This paper first constructs the optimal control model for FCFS scheduling policy, and further proposes a more practical model for DM scheduling policy.

div.head: C. Complexity
div.p: Since Lj is calculated off-line, the system overhead is mainly spent on monitoring the queue length for all types of tasks (Fig. 3). From (11), the computation of u depends only on the current queue length, so its complexity is a constant. Consequently, it is easy to implement the control system and it is quite practical.

div.head: IV. EXAMPLE ANALYSIS
div.p: In order to demonstrate that the proposed dynamic optimal control model is capable of adapting the QoS of incoming aperiodic tasks to the dynamically varying workload in order to quarantee the system timeliness and improve the throughput, we implement an example, based on the CRTOS II.

The example assumes the CPU provides 3 types of services that are corresponding to 3 different task deadlines: D1l=100ms, D2=200 ms, D3=400 ms, Consequently there are 3 priorities (N=3). Further, each type of tasks has 3 QoS levels (M=2). The task's arrival rates are respectively A1=40, )2=9,)3=15. let where uj,k is the service rate of the jth type of tasks with the kth QoS level. Let a=(0.7 0.2 0.1), b=(0.5 0.3 0.2). From ( 12), ( 14), (15), get L1=30, L2=12, L3=20. The monitors periodically sample the queue length for each type of tasks, and then the controllers determine the service rates that should be provided according to (1 1). Define a current task set V(t)={Ti: Ai < t <Ai + Dj±, which includes the tasks that have entered the system but their deadlines have not yet expired. Thus the current CPU utilization is:

In the example, both the incoming load and the actual CPU load can be described as utilization. The incoming load is defined as the sum of execution times of all arrived end-toend tasks over the time interval during which they arrived [5]. It is generated by a task generator implemented by C++, and its value is set around 150%. The example adopts the DM scheduling algorithm. Fig. 4 (a) and (b) respectively show the actual CPU utilization and the task's deadline miss ratio on the condition of using the dynamic optimal control and that not using the dynamic optimal control. It is seen that, when the dynamic optimal control is used, the CPU utilization almost reaches 100% while the deadline miss ratio is kept low enough. In contrast, when the dynamic optimal control is not used, the CPU utilization is merely 50% and the deadline miss ratio is relatively higher. This is caused by the random of the task arrivals and the unpredictability of task execution time. Therefore, the example indicates that, under the dynamic optimal control, the system performance is improved.

V. CONCLUSION The aperiodic soft RTS holds the characteristics of random and unpredictability. Traditional worst-case-based scheduling may lead to low CPU utilization or system overload. Moreover, the current random analysis methods are static and merely used for periodic task. This paper regards the aperiodic soft RTS as a queuing system, and then constructs a dynamic optimal control model that is capable of adjusting the task parameters according to the queue length. The model considers both the task's timeliness and it QoS level. Finally, an example demonstrates that the dynamic optimal control model can provide better performance for aperiodic soft RTS.
